title: When two wrongs make a right: The efficiency-consumption gap under separate vs. joint evaluations
research_question: How does the mode of evaluation (joint vs. separate) interact with the type of measure (efficiency vs. consumption) to influence people's judgments and willingness-to-pay (WTP) for upgrades, specifically in the context of the efficiency-consumption gap (ECG)? Can separate evaluation (SE) de-bias the errors people make when judging efficiency upgrades?

participants.description: Study 1: 1008 participants (Mage = 32.8, SDage = 11.7; 50% female) from the U.S., aged 18 or above, English as first language. Study 2: 748 participants (Mage = 34.72, SD = 12.8; 42.6% female) from the U.S., aged 18 or above, English as first language, did not participate in Study 1.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Study 1: Four hypothetical scenarios describing upgrades for consumer products/services: Internet speed (25 to 50 or 100 Mbps), driving speed (30 to 45 or 60 mph), printer speed (50 to 100 or 150 pages-per-minute), and car fuel efficiency (10 to 20 or 30 MPG). Each scenario presented two upgrade options (smaller vs. larger).

Study 2: One hypothetical scenario about using a fast lane for a 30-mile journey, presented in two versions: (1) higher driving speed (efficiency measure: 33, 36, 40, 45, 50, 55 mph) or (2) shorter journey time (consumption measure: 55, 50, 45, 40, 36, 33 minutes saved). Each version had six levels of upgrade.

measures.instrument: Slider scale (0 to $30, $50, $100, or $200 depending on scenario in Study 1; 0 to $30 in Study 2)

findings.antecedent: Upgrade size (small vs. large) for efficiency measures (Internet speed, driving speed, printer speed, fuel efficiency)
findings.mechanism: Interaction effect between evaluation mode (JE vs. SE) and upgrade size: WTP difference between small and large upgrades was much larger under JE than under SE.
findings.quote: In all four scenarios, the interactions between the mode (JE vs. SE) and the size of the upgrade (small vs. large) were statistically significant (p < .001).

findings.antecedent: Efficiency upgrades (Internet speed from 25 to 50 Mbps vs. 25 to 100 Mbps)
findings.mechanism: Under JE, WTP for larger upgrade (25-100 Mbps, M=$22.09) was about twice that for smaller upgrade (25-50 Mbps, M=$10.85). Under SE, WTP for larger upgrade (M=$17.60) was only 24% more than smaller upgrade (M=$14.24).
findings.quote: participants in the JE conditions were willing to pay about twice as much for upgrading their Internet speed from 25 to 100 vs. from 25 to 50 Mbps

findings.antecedent: Efficiency upgrades (driving speed, printer speed, fuel efficiency)
findings.mechanism: Under JE, WTP for larger upgrades was 70%-90% more than for smaller upgrades. Under SE, WTP for larger upgrades was only 13%-27% more than for smaller upgrades.
findings.quote: For the other three scenarios participants in the JE conditions were willing to pay 70%-90% more for the larger upgrade relative to the smaller upgrade

findings.antecedent: Efficiency upgrades (Internet speed, driving speed, printer speed, fuel efficiency)
findings.mechanism: Judgments were more biased (over-evaluation) in JE mode than in SE mode for efficiency upgrades, because actual savings follow a curvilinear function.
findings.quote: judgments were actually more biased in the JE mode than the SE mode.

findings.antecedent: Time saved (5 to 27 minutes) from driving speed or journey time upgrades
findings.mechanism: Under JE, WTP followed a monotonically increasing pattern with increasing time saved.
findings.quote: in the JE condition, participants' WTP followed a monotonically increasing pattern, as they were willing to pay marginally more for each speed increase or journey time decrease.

findings.antecedent: Measure type (speed vs. time) in JE condition
findings.mechanism: No main effect of whether the upgrade was presented as speed (efficiency) or time (consumption) on WTP in the JE condition.
findings.quote: no main effect for the measure (F(5,104) = 0.29, p = 0.92)

findings.antecedent: Time saved (5 to 27 minutes) from driving speed or journey time upgrades
findings.mechanism: Under SE, WTP was less sensitive to the degree of speed increased or amount of journey time reduced, but a significant effect for time saved was found overall.
findings.quote: in the SE condition the means of WTP participants indicated were much less sensitive to the degree of speed increased or amount of journey time reduced.

findings.antecedent: Measure type (speed vs. time) in SE condition
findings.mechanism: No significant effect of whether the upgrade was presented as speed (efficiency) or time (consumption) on WTP in the SE condition.
findings.quote: no significant effect for the measure (F(1,598) = 1.7, p = 0.19)

findings.antecedent: Time saved (5 to 27 minutes) in SE condition (speed measure scenario)
findings.mechanism: In the SE condition, when upgrades were presented as speed (efficiency measure), the amount of time saved had no significant effect on WTP.
findings.quote: the time saved had no significant effect in the speed measure scenario (F(5,301) = 0.85, p = 0.52).

findings.antecedent: Time saved (5 vs. 27 minutes) in SE condition (time measure scenario)
findings.mechanism: In the SE condition, when upgrades were presented as time saved (consumption measure), WTP was significantly different only between the extreme ends of the scale (5 vs. 27 minutes saved).
findings.quote: the effect of time saved was significant (F(5,297) = 2.69, p = 0.02), subsequent post-hoc tests showed the difference was only significant between the WTP for saving 5 minutes vs. 27 minutes

findings.mechanism: For consumption measures, subjective value under JE is less biased than under SE. JE preferences align with the linear objective value curve, while SE preferences follow a concave curve.
findings.quote: For consumption measures, the subjective value under JE is less biased than under SE

findings.mechanism: For efficiency measures, subjective value under SE is less biased than under JE. SE preferences align with the curvilinear objective value curve, while JE preferences follow a linear curve.
findings.quote: whereas for efficiency measures the opposite is true: judgments under SE are less biased than under JE.

mechanisms: The Efficiency-Consumption Gap (ECG) arises from people falsely believing that efficiency and consumption are linearly related, when they are curvilinear by definition. This leads to underestimation of impact from lower efficiency values and overestimation from higher values (MPG illusion, time-saving bias).

Evaluability theory (Hsee, 1998; Hsee & Zhang, 2004) suggests that under Joint Evaluation (JE), people are more sensitive to magnitude and follow a more linear subjective value function. Under Separate Evaluation (SE), people are less sensitive to magnitude and follow a flatter or concave subjective value function.

The 'two wrongs make a right' mechanism: When efficiency upgrades are judged under SE, the curvilinear (concave) subjective value function of SE aligns with the curvilinear (concave) objective value function of efficiency upgrades, leading to less biased preferences (WTP). This is not due to increased understanding of the non-linear relationship, but rather a coincidental negation of two biases.
moderators: Evaluation mode (Joint Evaluation vs. Separate Evaluation)
Measure type (efficiency measures vs. consumption measures)
implementation_implications: Policymakers and regulators should understand how evaluation modes affect decision-making in the context of the ECG to design policies that ensure consumers are afforded the most appropriate, and less biased, mode of evaluation when making judgments and decisions related to efficiency and consumption.
Consumers' awareness of their biased WTP in these contexts might assist them in reducing their susceptibility to overpaying for larger efficiency upgrades.
Overpaying for larger efficiency upgrades not only harms consumers but may also decrease innovation and adversely affect market efficiency.

tables.description: Predicted bias in WTP depending on measure and evaluation modes.
Means of WTP (and SDs) for the smaller and larger upgrades in joint vs. separate evaluations for the scenarios (Study 1).

limitations: Study 1 used only two value points (small vs. large upgrades), which is not enough to infer linear or curvilinear relationships definitively.
The studies focused only on upgrades, and future research should explore downgrades or choices between upgrades and downgrades.
The relative size of the upgrade compared to the initial point was not systematically manipulated across a wide range (e.g., 5% to 500% increases).
The findings do not imply that people become aware of the non-linear relationship under SE, only that their behavior is less biased.

paper_metadata.title: When two wrongs make a right: The efficiency-consumption gap under separate vs. joint evaluations
paper_metadata.crossref_title: When two wrongs make a right: The efficiency-consumption gap under separate vs. joint evaluations
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: AbstractThe MPG illusion and the time-saving bias both show that people misjudge the gains from increases in efficiency or speed, because people falsely believe that efficiency and speed are linearly related to consumption (e.g., gallons of fuel or journey time). This efficiency-consumption gap (ECG) has been demonstrated consistently in various situations. In parallel, people have also been found to show a diminished sensitivity to increases in magnitudes when judged under separate vs. joint evaluation modes (SE vs. JE). We show that these “two wrongs can make a right”: when people judge efficiency upgrades under SE mode, their subjective judgments follow a concave curve that closely resembles the curvilinear pattern of efficiency upgrades, making their preferences (artificially) less biased than they are under JE. In two studies we show that when asked for their willingness-to-pay (WTP) for upgrading products or services in two (a smaller vs. a larger) upgrade options, WTPs are less different in SE vs. JE modes. This means that people are exhibiting lower sensitivity to the upgrade size under SE which leads to a de-biasing effect. We show that because JE follow a linear trend, it yields biased preferences for efficiency measures, but not for consumption measures. In contrast, SE yield biased preferences for consumption, but not for efficiency measures.
